Given the arguments for both format-specificity and generalization, the degree of such cross-format consistency remains an open empirical question.

Modeling Extreme and Midpoint Responding Across Formats

Assessing the consistency of response styles across formats requires that they are operationalized in a comparable way. If the psychometric models used for the two response formats captured conceptually different tendencies, a low correlation could reflect differences between the models rather than format-specificity of response styles.

For Likert-type data, a wide range of models has been proposed (for overviews, see Böckenholt & Meiser, 2017; Henninger & Meiser, 2020a , 2020b). IRTree models decompose a response into sequential decisions, such as whether to choose the midpoint and whether to choose an extreme category, and thus treat midpoint and extreme responding as separate processes (Böckenholt, 2012; Plieninger & Meiser, 2014). Multidimensional nominal response models represent response styles as person-specific shifts in category-specific parameters (Bolt & Johnson, 2009; Falk & Cai, 2016). Jin and Wang (2014) proposed an extension of the partial credit model in which an additional latent dimension rescales the item thresholds: when the thresholds are compressed, extreme categories become more likely, and when they are widened, responses are drawn toward the middle of the scale. In this approach, extreme and midpoint responding form the two poles of a single continuous dimension.

For VAS, modeling approaches are considerably scarcer. Huang (2025) extended the continuous response model by a person parameter that shifts responses toward the extremes or the midpoint of the scale. Jiang et al. (2025) constructed pseudo-responses that reflect the distance of a response from the midpoint and modeled them jointly with the original responses, building on the zero-and one-inflated beta item response model (Molenaar et al., 2022). Vollbracht, Lischetzke, et al. (2026) extended the beta item response model (BIRM; Noel & Dauvier, 2007) by person-specific response style parameters. In its ERS extension (BIRM-ERS), a person parameter scales the difference between the latent trait and the item location, so that higher values shift responses farther from the center and toward the corresponding endpoint, whereas lower values shift them toward the center of the scale.

We argue that the model by Jin and Wang (2014) for Likert-type items and the BIRM-ERS for VAS items are the most closely aligned of the available approaches in their conceptualization of extreme and midpoint responding. 1 In both models, a single person parameter amplifies or attenuates deviations of responses from the center of the scale, while the direction of a response remains determined by the person's trait level relative to the item. 2Because no comparable operationalization of ARS is available for the model by Jin and Wang (2014), and to keep the joint model as parsimonious as possible, we focused the comparison on ERS.

The Present Study

We examined whether individual differences in extreme and midpoint responding generalize across Likert-type scales and VAS. To keep the comparison interpretable, we measured ERS, understood as a bipolar dimension from midpoint to extreme responding, in both formats with models that conceptualize it in the same way, and estimated them jointly in a preregistered within-subjects study. Based on the evidence that response styles are consistent 1 Treating extreme and midpoint responding as the poles of one dimension is an assumption of both models. For Likert-type data, approaches that model the two tendencies as separate processes (Böckenholt, 2012; Henninger & Meiser, 2020a) may capture aspects of midpoint responding that a single dimension does not, and the relative appropriateness of the two conceptualizations may vary across data sets (Schoenmakers et al., 2026). For VAS, no model that separates them has been established. When Jiang et al. (2025) evaluated such a specification, the two tendencies were almost perfectly negatively correlated (below -.97) across several empirical data sets. The authors attributed these strong negative correlations to characteristics of VAS responding and interpreted them as supporting the treatment of midpoint responding as the opposite pole of extreme responding. across traits, over time, and across numbers of response categories, we expected them to generalize across response formats as well: H1: Individual ERS estimates from the Likert-type items and the VAS items are positively related.

Because the two response formats require different psychometric models and crossformat consistency has not been examined directly, we did not specify an expected magnitude of the cross-format association but treated it as an open empirical question.

Method Participants

Participants were recruited via email distribution lists, social media, and printed flyers displayed at the university and in public places. Eligible participants were at least 18 years old and proficient in German. As compensation, participants could enter a raffle for one of 10 prizes of €100 or one of 20 prizes of €50; psychology students could alternatively receive course credit.

In addition, all participants could request a descriptive feedback report of their HEXACO results.

The preregistered target sample size was 500 analyzable data sets. In a pilot simulation study of the joint model described below, this sample size was sufficient to recover the crossformat correlation of ERS with only a small conservative bias. 3 In total, 655 participants gave informed consent and started the survey. Following the preregistered exclusion criteria, we excluded participants who did not complete the survey (n = 152) 4 and participants who indicated on the final page that they had not responded attentively and honestly (n = 2). The final sample consisted of N = 501 participants (69.7% female, 27.9% male, 2.0% non-binary, 0.4% not stated) aged 18 to 88 years (M = 38.5, SD = 17.2, Mdn = 31).

Participants completed the survey on a smartphone (56.7%), a computer (37.9%), or a tablet (5.4%).

Design and Procedure

The study used a within-subjects design in which each participant responded to one half of the HEXACO-PI-R items on a Likert-type scale and to the other half on a VAS. The 3 The simulation crossed two numbers of substantive dimensions per format (three and six) with four true cross-format correlations of ERS (0, .30, .60, and .90), with 100 replications per condition. Each data set comprised 500 persons and eight items per dimension and response format, with ERS variances of 0.3 (Likert-type) and 0.1 (VAS) and a cross-format trait correlation of .70 (all data-generating parameter values are reported in the Supplement). Across conditions, the bias of both the model-based and Spearman correlations ranged from -0.024 to 0.001 (Monte Carlo standard errors < 0.007), and 87% of the nominal 90% credible intervals contained the true value. Coverage was close to nominal for a true correlation of zero (93% and 92%) and lower for positive correlations (80% to 90%), suggesting that the credible intervals may be somewhat too narrow. The preregistration, the data and code of the present study, and the code and results of this simulation are available on the OSF at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MRP2Q. 4 Of these participants, 44 dropped out before the first item block, 74 during the first item block (42 in the Likert-type and 32 in the VAS block), 20 during the second item block (11 in the Likert-type and 9 in the VAS block), and 14 after both item blocks. assignment of items to formats was fixed and identical for all participants. The order of the two format blocks was randomized between participants, with 250 participants completing the Likerttype block first and 251 completing the VAS block first. We did not additionally counterbalance the assignment of items to formats, because this would have required approximately twice the sample size; instead, the two item subsets were balanced in content (see Measures section).

The survey was implemented in LimeSurvey (Version 6.17.13; LimeSurvey GmbH, 2026). After providing informed consent, participants reported their age, gender, and the device they were using. They then completed the two format blocks, each presented on two pages of 25 items in the original item order of the HEXACO-PI-R, followed by additional measures that were not part of the preregistered hypothesis and are not reported here (a self-concept clarity scale and items on response format preferences). On the final page, participants indicated whether they had responded attentively and honestly and were informed that their answer would have no consequences for them. The study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology at RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Measures

We used the German version of the HEXACO-PI-R (Lee & Ashton, 2018), which assesses the six HEXACO dimensions Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to Experience with 16 items each, organized into four facets per dimension (i.e., four items per facet), plus four interstitial Altruism items.

The 100 items were divided into two non-overlapping subsets of 50 items. The two subsets contained two items from each facet. In addition, the 60 items belonging to the HEXACO-60 were split evenly between the two subsets (30 items each). As far as these constraints allowed, the subsets were also balanced with respect to reverse-scored items, with the number of reversescored items differing by at most two per dimension. The four Altruism items were split evenly across the subsets and were not included in the psychometric models. The models thus comprised 48 items per response format, eight per dimension, of which 26 were reverse-scored in the Likert-type subset and 22 in the VAS subset. The assignment of each item to a format is documented in the codebook on the OSF.

The Likert-type items were presented with seven response categories, numbered from 1 to 7, with verbal labels only at the endpoints (strong disagreement and strong agreement). We used seven instead of the original five categories because a larger number of categories facilitates the identification of ERS with the model by Jin and Wang (2014). In the VAS format, items were presented as horizontal sliders with the same endpoint labels and no further labels, tick marks, or numeric values along the line. To avoid suggesting a default response, the slider had no initial handle position; the handle appeared only after participants clicked or tapped on the line.

Responses were recorded on a scale from 0 to 100, but participants never saw a numeric value corresponding to their response.

Data Preprocessing

Only participants who submitted the final page of the survey were retained, so the analyzed data contained no missing item responses. To check for straight-lining, we determined for each participant and response format the longest sequence of identical responses in the order of item presentation (two pages of 25 items per format). The longest sequence comprised nine Likert-type responses (one participant; all others at most six) and six VAS responses. Reversescored items were recoded prior to all analyses. Likert-type responses were used as ordered categories. VAS responses were rescaled from 0-100 to 0-1. Because the beta distribution is not defined at 0 and 1, rescaled VAS responses were truncated to the interval [0.0001, 0.9999] (Noel & Dauvier, 2007; Vollbracht, Lischetzke, et al., 2026). This affected 1,922 of 24,048 VAS responses (8.0%), all of which were exactly 0 or 100.

Statistical Analysis

To describe the data, we computed means, medians, and standard deviations of the scale scores for each HEXACO dimension, separately for the Likert-type and the VAS items. The preregistered hypothesis was tested with a psychometric response style model that incorporates responses from both formats, as described in the following sections.

Likert-Type Items

Responses to the Likert-type items were modeled with the extension of the partial credit model for extreme and midpoint responding proposed by Jin and Wang (2014), in which a person-specific parameter rescales the item thresholds around the item location to increase or decrease the probability of responding in the extreme categories. With the seven response categories recoded to 0, …, 6 and 𝑐 = 1, …, 6, the log-odds of responding in category 𝑐 rather where 𝜃 𝑖𝑘 𝑗 LIK is the trait of person 𝑖 on dimension 𝑘 𝑗 measured by item 𝑗 in the Likert-type format, 𝛿 𝑗 is the location (difficulty) of item 𝑗, and 𝜏 𝑗𝑐 is the 𝑐-th threshold of item 𝑗, centered such that ∑ 𝜏 𝑗𝑐 𝑐 = 0.

The term exp(-𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK ) acts as a person-specific multiplier of the centered thresholds.foot_2 For 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK > 0, the multiplier is smaller than one, and hence the thresholds move closer to the item location and the outer categories become more likely. For 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK < 0, the multiplier is larger than one, and hence the thresholds are spread apart and responses are drawn toward the middle categories. Because the item location is not rescaled, 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK affects only how spread out the responses are, whereas the direction of a response is determined by the trait relative to the item location. Higher values of 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK thus indicate stronger extreme responding and lower values indicate stronger midpoint responding.

VAS Items

Responses to the VAS items were modeled with the BIRM-ERS (Vollbracht, Lischetzke, et al., 2026), an extension of the beta item response model (Noel & Dauvier, 2007). Each rescaled response 𝑟 𝑖𝑗 ∈ (0,1) follows a beta distribution with shape parameters 𝑚 𝑖𝑗 = exp ( exp(𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS )(𝜃 𝑖𝑘 𝑗 VAS -𝛿 𝑗 )+𝜏 𝑗 2 ) , 𝑛 𝑖𝑗 = exp ( -exp(𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS )(𝜃 𝑖𝑘 𝑗 VAS -𝛿 𝑗 )+𝜏 𝑗 2 ) , (2) where 𝜃 𝑖𝑘 𝑗 VAS is the trait of person 𝑖 on dimension 𝑘 𝑗 measured by item 𝑗 in the VAS format, 𝛿 𝑗 is the location of item 𝑗, and 𝜏 𝑗 is its dispersion parameter. In this parameterization, log(𝑚 𝑖𝑗 /𝑛 𝑖𝑗 ) = exp(𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS ) (𝜃 𝑖𝑘 𝑗 VAS -𝛿 𝑗 ) determines the location of the response distribution, and log(𝑚 𝑖𝑗 𝑛 𝑖𝑗 ) = 𝜏 𝑗 determines its concentration, with higher values of 𝜏 𝑗 indicating less dispersed responses. The term exp(𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS ) scales the distance between the trait and the item location. For 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS > 0, this distance is amplified, and responses are shifted farther from the center, toward the upper endpoint when 𝜃 > 𝛿 and toward the lower endpoint when 𝜃 < 𝛿. For 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS < 0, the distance is attenuated, and responses are drawn toward the center of the scale.

As in the Likert-type model, the response style parameter thus changes how extreme a response is but not its direction. For numerical stability, the arguments of the outer exponential functions were constrained to the interval [-7, 7].foot_3

Joint Model for Likert-Type and VAS Responses

The parameters of each person were collected in a vector 𝛏 𝑖 of length 2𝐷 + 2, comprising the 𝐷 = 6 Likert-type traits, the 𝐷 VAS traits, and the two response style parameters 𝜂 𝑖 and 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS .

ERS,LIK

These vectors followed a common multivariate normal distribution with a mean vector of zero, a vector of standard deviations 𝛔, and a correlation matrix 𝐑:

The correlation matrix describes the associations among all traits and response styles within and across formats. The cross-format correlation of ERS, 𝜌 ERS = 𝐑[𝜂 ERS,LIK , 𝜂 ERS,VAS ], which tests H1, is thus a parameter of the model. Estimating the two models jointly avoids correlating point estimates: person estimates from separately fitted models contain measurement error and are shrunken toward the mean, so that their correlation is generally a biased estimate of the correlation between the underlying person parameters (Rouder & Haaf, 2019). Because higher values of both response style parameters indicate stronger extreme responding, a positive correlation means that participants who respond more extremely than others on the Likert-type items also do so on the VAS items. As preregistered, the order of the format blocks was not included in the model.

We specified an LKJ(2) prior on 𝐑 and normal priors truncated at zero on the standard deviations: 𝒩 + (1,0.2) for the Likert-type traits and 𝒩 + (0,1) for the VAS traits and both response style parameters. Because the response style parameters enter the two models in exponentiated form, their standard deviations refer to the log scale. The LKJ(2) prior is symmetric around zero and places less density on correlations close to -1 and 1 than a uniform prior over correlation matrices, without ruling out substantial correlations. The informative prior on the Likert-type trait standard deviations was adapted from Jin and Wang (2014). 7 Item locations (in both formats) and Likert-type thresholds received weakly informative 𝒩(0,3) priors, and the VAS dispersion parameters received a 𝒩(1,2) prior truncated at 0.1. This constraint prevents the two shape parameters from both falling below one, which would result in 7 Jin and Wang (2014) fixed the trait distribution to a standard normal distribution for model identification. Because the item slopes of the partial credit model are fixed, however, this constraint is not required for identification in the present model. In the main analysis, the posterior medians of the standard deviations of the Likert-type traits ranged from 0.33 to 0.52 and were thus considerably lower than the mean of their prior distribution. In a sensitivity analysis with a weakly informative 𝒩 + (0,1) prior, these standard deviations ranged from 0.33 to 0.51, the cross-format correlation of ERS was 𝜌 ERS = .76, 95% CrI [.67, .83], and the Spearman rank correlation was 𝑟 𝑠 = .75, 95% CrI [.68, .81]. The conclusions thus did not change.

a U-shaped beta density, with its mass concentrated at the two endpoints. Person parameters were estimated with a non-centered parameterization. each model. Both parameters capture the same tendency, but they are not fully equivalent, and the figure shows where they diverge. When a person's trait equals the item location (𝜃 = 𝛿), compressed thresholds in the Likert-type model make both outer categories more likely, so that extreme responding manifests in both directions.

Conceptual Comparison of the Response Style Parameters

In the BIRM-ERS, the response style parameter only scales an existing deviation between trait and item location and therefore has no effect when 𝜃 = 𝛿. Extreme responding on the VAS is thus represented as a tendency to respond more extremely in the direction implied by the trait, whereas on the Likert-type scale it additionally spreads responses toward both outer categories when the trait is close to the item location.

Estimation and Inference

The model was estimated in Stan via CmdStan (Version 2.36.0; Stan Development Team, 2026)foot_4 and the R package cmdstanr (Version 0.9.0; Gabry et al., 2025) in R (Version 4.6.1; R Core Team, 2026). We ran four chains with 1,500 warmup and 3,000 sampling iterations each, a target acceptance rate of .90, and a maximum tree depth of 12. Convergence was evaluated with 𝑅 ̂ (criterion: 𝑅 ̂< 1.01), bulk and tail effective sample sizes (Vehtari et al., 2021), and the absence of divergent transitions.

We report posterior medians and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). H1 was considered supported if the 95% CrI of 𝜌 ERS lay entirely above zero. Because the latent scales of the two models need not be linearly related, we applied the same criterion to the Spearman rank correlation (𝑟 𝑠 ) between 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK and 𝜂 𝑖 ERS,VAS , computed across persons within each posterior draw. Model fit was evaluated with posterior predictive checks. For 1,000 posterior draws, we replicated the responses of all participants from the fitted model and compared features of the observed data with their replicated distributions, including the proportion of extreme responses, within-person response variability, and the cross-format association of response extremity.

Exploratory and Sensitivity Analyses

As additional exploratory and sensitivity analyses that were not preregistered, we examined how the cross-format correlation of ERS compares with the consistency of ERS within each format and whether it depended on the truncation of the VAS endpoint responses, acquiescence, or the device used.

To obtain a within-format benchmark, we split the 48 items of each format into two halves of 24 items (A and B), following the rules used to split the HEXACO-PI-R items between the formats: each half contained one item per facet and half of the format's HEXACO-60 items, and the halves were balanced as far as possible with respect to reverse-scored items. We then fitted one joint model in which each of the four item sets had its own six traits and its own ERS parameter. 9 The 28 person parameters followed one multivariate normal distribution, so that the model yields the correlations of ERS between the halves within each format and across formats, each based on 24 items per parameter.

To examine whether the results depended on the truncation of the VAS endpoint responses, we refitted the joint model with the endpoint responses truncated to [0.001, 0.999] and to [0.005, 0.995] instead of [0.0001, 0.9999], with all other settings as in the main analysis.

To examine whether acquiescence affected the results, we computed a simple acquiescence index for each response format, because no comparable ARS component is available for the Likert-type model. The index was based on the item responses rescaled to a range of 0 to 1 without recoding the reverse-scored items. For each dimension, we averaged the mean response to the regular items and the mean response to the reverse-scored items, so that the trait largely cancels out. We then averaged these values across the six dimensions (cf. Soto et al., 2008). Higher values indicate a stronger tendency to agree irrespective of item content.

To examine whether the device affected the results, we compared endpoint use and the ERS parameters between participants who used a smartphone and participants who used a computer.

Partial correlations of ERS across response formats were computed as Spearman rank correlations of the person parameters of the main analysis within each posterior draw, so that their posterior distributions reflect the uncertainty in the person parameters.

Results

Descriptive Statistics

Table 1 shows descriptive statistics for the HEXACO scale scores in both formats.

Internal consistencies (𝛼) ranged from .59 to .79, which is to be expected for eight-item scales covering four heterogeneous facets. 10 Scale scores of the same dimension correlated between .71 and .85 across formats, whereas all other scale intercorrelations were small (|r| ≤ .27). Mean differences between formats are not interpretable as format effects because format and item subset were confounded by design.

In the Likert-type format, 6.1% of the responses fell into the lowest and 19.0% into the highest category. In the VAS format, 2.0% of the responses were exactly 0 and 6.0% were exactly 100, and 72% of participants used an endpoint at least once. At the person level, the proportion of extreme categories in the Likert-type format (M = .25, SD = .14) and the mean 10 In six-factor confirmatory factor analyses conducted separately for each format with MLR estimation in lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), essential 𝜏-equivalence was rejected for both formats (Likert-type: scaled 𝛥𝜒 2 (42) = 137.8; VAS: scaled 𝛥𝜒 2 (42) = 283.4; both p < .001), and the congeneric models also showed poor fit, which is to be expected for scales that combine four facets. Coefficient 𝛼 should therefore be interpreted with caution; it differed from McDonald's 𝜔 by less than .02.

distance of VAS responses from the midpoint (M = 27.3, SD = 5.2) were substantially correlated (𝑟 𝑠 = .65; Figure 2, left panel).foot_6

Convergence

All preregistered convergence criteria were met. There were no divergent transitions and no transitions exceeding the maximum tree depth, and the minimum E-BFMI was .69. For all correlations and standard deviations reported below, 𝑅 ̂ was at most 1.002, and bulk and tail effective sample sizes were at least 2,642 and 4,394, respectively.

Posterior Predictive Checks

The model reproduced the item means and the overall response distributions well. Only one of the 96 item means fell outside its 95% posterior predictive interval, the observed proportions of the Likert-type categories deviated by at most 1.1 percentage points from their replicated medians, and the proportions of VAS responses in ten equally wide bins deviated by at most 2.2 percentage points.

However, the model systematically underestimated between-person differences in response extremity (Table 2). In both formats, the observed standard deviations across participants of the extreme response indicators and of within-person response variability exceeded the replicated values. Accordingly, more participants than expected fell outside their 95% posterior predictive intervals for the VAS distance from the midpoint (21.6%), the withinperson VAS standard deviation (24.8%), and the proportion of Likert-type midpoint responses (16.6%), compared with the approximately 5% expected under good model fit. The model also underestimated the proportion of VAS responses close to the endpoints.

Cross-Format Consistency of ERS

The posterior median of the cross-format correlation of ERS was 𝜌 ERS = .76, 95% CrI with small negative correlations with Emotionality in both formats. The full correlation matrix of the person parameters is reported in the Supplement. In the posterior predictive checks (Table 2), the association between the two observed extremity indicators was weaker in the replicated data than in the observed data.

For comparison, the cross-format correlations of the substantive traits ranged from .89 to .97, exceeding the correlations of the observed scale scores. The same pattern held for ERS, for which the model-based correlation (𝜌 ERS = .76) exceeded the correlation of the two observed extremity indicators reported above (𝑟 𝑠 = .65; Figure 2, left panel).

Exploratory and Sensitivity Analyses

All additional models met the preregistered convergence criteria.

Within-Format Benchmark

Within formats, the ERS parameters of the two halves correlated at .88, 95% CrI [.82, .93] (Likert-type) and .77, 95% CrI [.68, .84] (VAS; all correlations are reported in the Supplement).

Across formats, the four correlations between halves were somewhat lower, ranging from .63 to .70. The Spearman rank correlations and a fit with the preregistered prior led to the same results. For the substantive traits, the correlations between halves did not differ systematically between formats (.61 to .89).

Truncation of VAS Endpoint Responses

With a truncation constant of 0.001, the cross-format correlation of ERS was 𝜌 ERS = .79, 95% CrI [.70, .86], and with a truncation constant of 0.005, it was 𝜌 ERS = .80, 95% CrI [.71, .87] (main analysis: 𝜌 ERS = .76). Fewer dispersion parameters were close to their lower bound ( 16and 11 of 48 items, compared with 26), whereas the rank order of the participants on the VAS ERS parameter was hardly affected (𝑟 𝑠 ≥ .97 between the posterior means).

Acquiescence

The acquiescence indices correlated only weakly across formats (𝑟 𝑠 = .27), and their correlations with the ERS parameters of either format ranged from -.05 to .05. Controlling for both indices changed the cross-format correlation of ERS only marginally (partial 𝑟 𝑠 = .75, 95% CrI [.68, .82]). The simple mean of the unrecoded responses led to the same results.

Device

Participants who used a smartphone gave slightly more VAS endpoint responses than participants who used a computer (8.6% vs. 7.2%), but their responses were, on average, less extreme in both formats. Controlling for the device changed the cross-format correlation of ERS only marginally (partial 𝑟 𝑠 = .75, 95% CrI [.68, .81]). Because participants chose the device themselves, these differences may also reflect characteristics of the participants rather than of the device.

Discussion

In a within-subjects study, we examined whether individual differences in extreme and midpoint responding generalize across Likert-type scales and VAS. Using conceptually aligned response style models for both formats that were estimated jointly, we found a substantial crossformat correlation of ERS (𝜌 ERS = .76). The Spearman rank correlation led to the same conclusion. Individual differences in extreme responding thus generalized to a considerable extent across response formats.

Response Styles Across Response Formats

The results extend previous evidence on the consistency of response styles across traits (Wetzel et al., 2013), over time (Weijters, Geuens, et al., 2010b; Wetzel et al., 2016), and across rating scales with different numbers of categories (Kieruj & Moors, 2013) to response formats that differ fundamentally in how responses are given. Although VAS have no discrete categories and no marked midpoint, participants who preferred the outer categories of a Likert-type scale also tended to place their VAS responses farther from the center of the scale. This pattern is in line with the view that ERS reflects, at least in part, a stable characteristic of the person rather than a reaction to a specific response format (Wetzel et al., 2016).

At the same time, the correlation was clearly below one. We deliberately did not specify an expected magnitude, but the shared variance of approximately 58% is in the same general range as the proportion of variance in response style factors that Wetzel et al. (2016) attributed to stable trait components over eight years (49% to 59%), even though the two indices are not directly comparable. A more direct benchmark comes from the split-half analysis. ERS was not perfectly consistent within a format either: the two halves of the same format correlated at .88 (Likert-type) and .77 (VAS). Part of the gap between 𝜌 ERS and one thus reflects differences between item sets rather than the response format. Between halves of different formats, the four correlations (.63 to .70) were somewhat lower than the within-format correlations, particularly than the one for the Likert-type format. Because the within-format correlations are themselves model-based estimates and do not mark an upper limit for the cross-format consistency, this comparison cannot quantify the format effect, but it suggests that this effect is not large.

Nevertheless, a considerable part of the individual differences in extreme responding was not shared across formats and item sets. This part may reflect processes that differ between formats, such as the mapping of a judgment onto discrete categories versus a continuous line, the handling of the slider, or the use of the endpoints. However, it may also partly result from the models themselves, whose two response style parameters are not fully equivalent (see below).

Practically, these findings imply that switching from Likert-type scales to VAS does not remove individual differences in extreme responding. Response styles should therefore be taken into account in VAS data as well. In addition, the substantial cross-format consistency suggests that ERS estimates from one format carry information about response behavior in the other, which may be relevant when questionnaires combine both formats.

Methodological Implications

Estimating the cross-format correlation within a joint model avoided the pitfalls of correlating point estimates. In our data, the correlation of the posterior means of the two response style parameters (r = .88) was considerably higher than the model-based correlation. In the joint model, each person's estimate in one format is informed by their responses in the other format via the estimated correlation, which pulls the two point estimates toward each other. Correlations of separately estimated point estimates, in contrast, tend to be attenuated by measurement error (Rouder & Haaf, 2019). In both cases, the correlation of point estimates is a biased estimate of the association of interest, whereas 𝜌 ERS is estimated with the uncertainty in the person parameters taken into account.

The posterior predictive checks showed what the ERS parameterization does and does not capture. In data replicated from the model, the two extremity indicators were less strongly related than in the observed data, so the model reproduced the cross-format association only in part. The substantial correlation is therefore not simply an artifact of the model structure. However, the weaker replicated association at least partly reflects that extremity varied less between participants in the replicated than in the observed data (Table 2), indicating that the model does not capture all individual differences in extremity.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations should be considered. First, both models treat extreme and midpoint responding as opposite poles of a single dimension, which we have referred to as ERS throughout. The underestimated heterogeneity in midpoint responses suggests that this assumption does not fully hold, so that our evidence mainly concerns the extreme pole. Models that separate the two tendencies (Böckenholt, 2012; Henninger & Meiser, 2020a) could clarify whether midpoint responding generalizes across formats to the same extent, and model comparisons could indicate which conceptualization fits the data better (Schoenmakers et al., 2026). For VAS, this would first require a specification in which the two tendencies are empirically separable, which the existing approach did not achieve (Jiang et al., 2025).

Second, the two response style parameters are not fully equivalent (see Figure 1).

In the BIRM-ERS, ERS amplifies only existing deviations between trait and item location, whereas in the model by Jin and Wang (2014), it additionally spreads responses toward both outer categories when the trait is close to the item location. This difference may contribute to the imperfect cross-format correlation and possibly to the underestimated heterogeneity in VAS extremity. A fully identical operationalization is not possible, however, because Likert-type and VAS responses differ in their structure and therefore require different measurement models, including different response style models: applying a model for ordered categories to VAS responses would require an arbitrary categorization that determines what counts as an extreme response, and applying a model for continuous responses to Likert-type responses would treat ordered categories as interval-scaled data. Response format and measurement model are therefore necessarily confounded, so that differences between the formats cannot be separated from differences between the models, including in the split-half analysis.

A substantial crossformat correlation that is merely an artifact of the models would, in turn, require both parameters to capture a common source of variance other than ERS. The additional analyses provided no indication of such a source: the ERS parameters were largely unrelated to the substantive traits, and controlling for acquiescence or the device changed the cross-format correlation only marginally. Moreover, the observed extremity indicators, which do not depend on either model, were also substantially correlated.

Third, endpoint responses on the VAS had to be truncated because the beta distribution is not defined at 0 and 1, and the model underestimated their frequency. The truncated endpoint responses also affected the item parameters: for 26 of the 48 VAS items, the posterior median of the dispersion parameter was below 0.15 and thus close to its lower bound of 0.1, and the dispersion parameters were lower (i.e., responses were more dispersed) the more endpoint responses an item received (𝑟 𝑠 = -.79). With larger truncation constants, fewer dispersion parameters were close to their bound and the cross-format correlation was slightly higher (.79 and .80), whereas the rank order of the participants on the VAS ERS parameter was hardly affected. The choice of the truncation constant thus did not change the conclusions. A zero-and one-inflated extension of the BIRM-ERS (cf. Molenaar et al., 2022) in which the same ERS parameter governs both the dispersion of continuous responses and the probability of endpoint responses would parallel the Likert-type model more closely and remove the need for truncation.

Such a model would also allow testing whether endpoint use and extremity within the range of the VAS reflect the same tendency, by comparing a variant in which one ERS parameter governs both parts with a variant with two correlated person parameters. However, although linking endpoint responses to response style parameters has been suggested (Vollbracht, Lischetzke, et al., 2026), such an extension of the BIRM-ERS has not yet been developed. Jiang et al. (2025) accommodated endpoint responses within a zero-and one-inflated framework, but they operationalized ERS through pseudo-responses rather than as a parameter that scales the response distribution, so that using their model would have sacrificed the conceptual alignment with the Likert-type model on which the present comparison rests. For an extension of the BIRM-ERS, it is not evident how ERS should enter the inflation terms, for example, whether it should increase the probability of endpoint responses regardless of the trait or only in the direction implied by the trait relative to the item. Moreover, the recovery of person parameters for endpoint use, which would be based on comparatively few endpoint responses per person, would first need to be established in simulations.

Fourth, both formats were administered in a single session. Shared state influences, such as motivation or carefulness on that day, may have contributed to the consistency, so our findings concern consistency across formats within one assessment rather than stability across occasions. The order of the two format blocks was randomized and was only weakly related to the extremity indicators, so order effects are unlikely to account for the association. Fifth, apart from excluding participants who indicated that they had not responded attentively and honestly and checking for straight-lining, we did not screen for other forms of careless responding, and response times were not recorded. Careless responding that manifests similarly in both formats, Although this confound is unlikely to affect the correlation of the response style parameters, it precludes interpreting mean differences between formats.

Taken together, these limitations point to three directions for future work. On the modeling side, the VAS extension outlined above would remove the need for truncation, whereas on the Likert-type side an operationalization of ARS within the same threshold-scaling logic would be needed to extend the comparison beyond ERS. A second direction is to relax the conceptual alignment deliberately: comparing formats with models that conceptualize response styles differently would show how much of the cross-format correlation depends on the alignment we imposed. Finally, the question of cross-format consistency is of particular relevance in settings in which VAS are common, such as ambulatory assessment (Vollbracht, Ottenstein, et al., 2026). In such data, ERS has been found to be associated with within-person variability in affect ratings (Henninger et al., 2026), and response styles could be studied across formats and across many repeated measurements.

Conclusion

ERS showed substantial consistency across Likert-type scales and VAS (𝜌 ERS = .76, 95% CrI [.68, .83]), indicating that individual differences in extreme responding generalize to a considerable extent across response formats. Response styles should therefore be considered regardless of the response format, and conceptually aligned models estimated jointly offer a way to study them across formats. Because both credible intervals lay entirely above zero, H1 was supported by both measures. The posterior probability that 𝜌 ERS exceeded .50 was > .999. The width of the credible interval of 𝜌 ERS was 0.15. A correlation of .76 corresponds to approximately 58% shared variance between the ERS parameters across formats. The standard deviations of the response style parameters were SD = 0.64, 95% CrI [0.57, 0.72] for the Likerttype format and SD = 0.37, 95% CrI [0.34, 0.41] for the VAS format, indicating individual differences in ERS in both formats. Because the two parameters are defined on different scales, their standard deviations are not directly comparable. The empirical reliability of the individual ERS parameters, that is, the variance of their posterior means divided by the sum of this variance and the mean posterior variance, was .76 for the Likert-type format and .75 for the VAS format (traits: .76 to .86). The ERS parameters were largely unrelated to the substantive traits (|𝜌| ≤ .24), such as repeatedly choosing the endpoints, might inflate the cross-format consistency.

Careless responding confined to one format would work in the opposite direction. However, evidence as to which format elicits more careless responding is mixed: Zhang et al. (2025) found a higher proportion of careless respondents in VAS than in Likert-type data, whereas Ulitzsch et al. (2026) found slightly higher rates of careless responding for Likert-type scales in ambulatory assessment. Because the beta mixture model of Zhang et al. (2025) builds on the same measurement model as the BIRM-ERS, modeling careless responding and response styles jointly across formats is a feasible next step. Finally, the assignment of items to formats was fixed.

Selected Posterior Predictive Checks

We preferred the BIRM-ERS over the extension of the continuous response model byHuang (2025) because the BIRM-ERS does not require an additional scaling parameter. Both approaches showed satisfactory parameter recovery in simulations(Huang, 2025; Vollbracht, Lischetzke, et al., 2026). For the BIRM-ERS, recovery of the ERS parameter was largely unaffected by sample size, and the model converged without difficulties with respondents.

In an empirical application, models including response style parameters also fit VAS data better than models without such parameters(Vollbracht, Lischetzke, et al., 2026).

In the original formulation, the multiplier is a lognormally distributed person parameter 𝜔 𝑖 , with values below one indicating extreme responding and values above one indicating midpoint responding(Jin & Wang, 2014). Writing it as 𝜔 𝑖 = exp(-𝜂 𝑖 ERS,LIK ) leaves the model unchanged but reverses the direction of the latent variable, such that higher values indicate stronger extreme responding, as is the case in the BIRM-ERS for VAS. The response style parameters in the extended partial credit model for Likert-type items and the BIRM-ERS for VAS therefore point in the same direction, such that a positive correlation between them indicates cross-format consistency in extreme versus midpoint responding.

This constraint serves numerical stability during sampling and is unrelated to the truncation of endpoint responses described above. It was never active: across all posterior draws, persons, and items, the largest absolute argument was 4.6.

The preregistration specified Stan Version 2.39, which was not available on the computing cluster used for estimation.

As in the main analysis, we used an LKJ(2) prior for the correlation matrix. However, as the results of the main analysis showed, the standard deviations of the Likert-type traits were considerably lower than the mean of their preregistered prior distribution. Because this prior would carry more weight with only four items per trait, we used the weakly informative 𝒩 + (0,1) prior for all trait standard deviations in this model and repeated the analysis with the preregistered prior as a sensitivity check.

This association did not depend on two features of the administration: the order of the format blocks was only weakly related to the two indicators (|d| ≤ 0.12), and the association was similar for participants who used a computer (𝑟 𝑠 = .67) or a smartphone (𝑟 𝑠 = .66); the tablet group was too small for a separate estimate (n = 27).
